The next phase is sharper: building a globally relevant, AI-native company where every function compounds leverage, not headcount. Join us as we continue to shape the sound of tomorrow! Your Will Bes We are looking for an experienced and hands-on Senior Manager - Aftersales Operations to own and drive the end-to-end Repair, Replacement, QC, Product Testing and Dispatch Operations across Audio, Wearables and other consumer electronics categories. The role will be responsible for ensuring that products received through customer returns, service centres, warehouses and other channels are accurately received, inspected, tested, repaired/replaced where applicable, dispositioned and dispatched within defined TATs, along with management of spares and inventory through the OMS platform. The individual will work closely with Customer Experience, Warehouse, Inventory, Logistics, Quality, Product, Technology and external service partners to ensure seamless execution of the aftersales lifecycle. This role requires a strong combination of operations management, technical understanding, QC expertise, inventory discipline, data analysis, process improvement and people leadership. 1. End-to-End Repair Replacement Operations Own the complete repair and replacement lifecycle from receipt of returned/defective products to final closure. Define and manage processes for product receiving, physical verification, serial number validation, QC inspection, functional testing, repair assessment, replacement approval, product disposition, inventory reconciliation and final dispatch through CRM. Establish clear SOPs and process controls to minimize leakage, delays, wrong replacements and incorrect dispositions. Ensure replacement products are dispatched within committed customer TAT. 2. Product QC Testing - Audio, Wearables Other Categories Own pre-dispatch and post-return QC/testing for Audio, Wearables and other consumer electronics categories. Define category-wise testing protocols and checklists for TWS/Earbuds, Headphones/Neckbands, Speakers/Audio products, Smartwatches/Smart Bands, Power Banks and other electronic accessories and NPD categories. Ensure complete functional testing before replacement dispatch, refurbishment, restocking, repair closure or customer shipment. Build testing parameters covering battery performance, charging, Bluetooth/pairing, audio output, microphone, touch/buttons, sensors, display, connectivity, app synchronization, physical condition, accessories and packaging. Ensure products failing QC are correctly segregated and do not enter saleable/replacement inventory. Continuously improve testing methodology based on emerging customer complaints and product defect trends. 3. Replacement Product Dispatch Management Own replacement dispatch readiness and ensure only QC-approved products are dispatched. Maintain controls around product model, SKU, serial number, colour/variant, product condition, accessories and packaging. Coordinate with Warehouse and Inventory teams to ensure replacement stock is available and accurately reflected in the system. Establish daily dispatch plans based on ageing and customer commitment. Track pending replacement cases and ensure there are no avoidable ageing cases. Identify bottlenecks causing delays in replacement dispatch and implement corrective actions. 4. TAT Management Own and monitor end-to-end aftersales TAT across receiving, QC, repair, replacement and dispatch. Define stage-wise TATs and SLAs for product receiving, QC inspection, technical testing, repair assessment, replacement approval, inventory allocation and dispatch. Maintain daily ageing dashboards and ensure cases crossing SLA are immediately escalated. Drive a culture of zero avoidable ageing within the team. Identify root causes of TAT breaches and implement preventive measures. Publish daily/weekly TAT performance reports to senior leadership. Key TAT Metrics tracked: Overall Repair TAT, Replacement TAT, QC TAT; Receiving-to-QC TAT, QC-to-Dispatch TAT; Average Ageing, Cases > SLA; First-Time-Right QC %, Dispatch SLA adherence %. 5. Returns Reverse Logistics Management Own the operational strategy for products returning from customers, service centres, marketplaces and other channels. Analyse return volumes and identify major drivers. Ensure returned products are correctly classified into Repairable, Replaceable, NTF/No Trouble Found, Physical Damage, Liquid Damage, Manufacturing Defect, Refurbishable, Scrap/Non-recoverable and Restockable. Ensure proper disposition and system closure of every returned unit. Work with Logistics and Warehouse teams to reduce reverse-logistics TAT and cost. 6. Root Cause Analysis Defect Reduction Analyse product return and QC data to identify recurring product and process failures. Build RCA dashboards covering top complaint reasons, top defective SKUs, product/category-wise failure rates, NTF %, repeat failure %, repair failure %, QC rejection %, replacement rate and return rate. Partner with Product, Quality, Engineering and NPD teams to identify systemic product issues. Convert customer complaint data into actionable product improvement recommendations. Track corrective and preventive actions until closure. Identify opportunities to reduce unnecessary replacements, repairs and returns. 7. Customer Experience Partnership Work closely with Customer Experience / Customer Service leadership to ensure operational issues do not negatively impact customer experience. Create clear escalation mechanisms between CX and Aftersales Operations. Ensure customer commitments made by CX teams are operationally achievable and tracked. Provide CX teams with accurate visibility on product availability, repair status, replacement status, QC status, dispatch status and expected TAT. Support CX escalations involving delayed repairs, replacement delays, product quality concerns and exceptional cases. 8. Warehouse Inventory Management Partner closely with Warehouse and Inventory teams to maintain 100% stock accuracy for repair and replacement inventory. Ensure proper segregation of fresh stock, replacement stock, returned stock, repairable stock, refurbished stock, QC hold stock, defective stock and scrap stock. Monitor physical vs system inventory reconciliation. Ensure no product is dispatched without appropriate system and QC clearance. Minimize inventory ageing and unidentified inventory. Establish controls for serial-number-level inventory tracking. 9. Team Management Leadership Lead and manage QC Engineers, QC Specialists, Inventory Associates and Aftersales Operations Associates. Define manpower requirements based on business volumes and workload. Hire, train, coach and develop team members. Establish individual and team-level performance KPIs. Conduct regular performance reviews and provide structured feedback. Manage daily manpower planning and workload allocation. Ensure adequate staffing during peak periods and product launches. Build technical capability within the QC team through regular training and certification. Establish accountability at individual process stages. 10. Process Excellence Automation Continuously identify opportunities to simplify and automate aftersales processes. Work with Technology/Product/Engineering teams to improve RMS and internal systems. Drive automation for product receiving, serial number validation, QC status, inventory movement, repair tracking, replacement allocation, dispatch readiness, TAT alerts, ageing alerts and reporting dashboards. Eliminate manual trackers wherever system-based solutions are feasible. Develop robust SOPs, process maps, escalation matrices and control mechanisms. 11. Cost Management Identify opportunities to reduce the cost of repairs, replacements, reverse logistics, packaging, inventory handling, manpower, refurbishment and scrap. Monitor cost per return, cost per repair and cost per replacement. Reduce unnecessary replacements through better diagnosis and testing. Improve recovery from returned products through refurbishment/restocking wherever commercially and operationally viable. Track savings generated through process improvement initiatives. 12. Escalation Exception Management Own critical operational escalations related to delayed replacements, delayed repairs, QC disputes, wrong product dispatch, inventory mismatch, repeated product failures, customer escalations and partner/service-centre disputes. Establish an escalation matrix with clear ownership and resolution timelines. Ensure high-priority cases receive immediate action and do not age unnecessarily. Work with CX leadership on customer-sensitive cases requiring exceptional intervention. 13. MIS, Analytics Senior Management Reporting Daily dashboards covering: products received, products under QC, QC completed; repair pending, replacement pending, dispatch pending; cases ageing beyond SLA, inventory availability and QC rejection rate. Weekly/Monthly dashboards covering: return rate, replacement rate, repair rate, NTF %; QC pass %, QC rejection %, restock rate, refurbishment recovery %; average TAT, SLA adherence; cost per return, cost per repair, cost per replacement; product/category-wise defect trends, top RCA drivers and team productivity. Present actionable insights to senior management rather than only reporting numbers - highlighting key risks, gaps, corrective actions and expected business impact. The Ideal Noisemaker 10-12+ years of relevant experience in Aftersales, Repair Operations, QC, Returns, Reverse Logistics, Warehouse Operations or Consumer Electronics. Experience managing Audio, Wearables, Mobile Accessories or consumer electronics preferred. Experience managing QC/testing teams and warehouse/inventory operations. Strong experience in Repair Replacement / RMA / Returns Management. Experience working with RMS/WMS or other inventory and aftersales systems. Strong understanding of consumer electronics QC and testing, and the ability to define QC protocols and testing checklists. Strong knowledge of inventory, reverse logistics, and serial-number/SKU-level inventory management. Strong knowledge of TAT/SLA management, with strong analytical and problem-solving capability. Advanced Excel / Google Sheets skills, with experience creating operational dashboards and MIS. Strong people-management, team-building and stakeholder-management skills - able to work with CX, Warehouse, Logistics, Product, Quality and Technology teams. Strong communication and presentation skills, with the ability to operate effectively in a high-volume, fast-paced environment. Key Performance Indicators Replacement TAT Repair TAT - maintain agreed SLA. QC TAT - same-day / defined SLA adherence. Dispatch TAT - timely dispatch of QC-approved units. SLA Adherence - maximize; Ageing Cases - minimize. QC Accuracy First-Time-Right QC - maximize. Inventory Accuracy - 100% system vs physical reconciliation. NTF % - reduce through better diagnosis. Return Rate - reduce through RCA; Restock Rate - improve where applicable. Cost per Return / Cost per Repair - reduce and optimize. Replacement Leakage - minimize. Team Productivity - improve; Process Compliance - 100% adherence. Leadership Expectations The successful candidate will be expected to operate as the owner of Aftersales Operations, not merely as a process manager. The individual should be able to: Identify operational gaps independently and build scalable processes from the ground up. Use data to identify problems and drive decisions. Balance Customer Experience, Quality, TAT and Cost. Build strong accountability within the team, and challenge existing processes to continuously improve them. Convert recurring customer complaints into operational and product improvements. Drive cross-functional projects to closure, and build systems and processes that can scale with business growth. title: RBI Data Analysis
description:
Job Summary Credit Risk in Indian Banking: RBI Data Analysis For most of the last decade, credit risk in Indian banking meant a crisis story. Ballooning bad loans. Undercapitalised public sector banks. A system searching for a floor. That story has changed. This analysis of Indian banking credit risk data draws straight from RBI s own numbers. It shows a sector operating at some of the lowest stressed-asset levels in its history. At the same time, new risks are quietly building underneath: unsecured retail credit, gold loans, and a fast-growing NBFC sector. So for anyone building credit risk models on Indian data, the headline ratio matters less than the underlying trend. What matters is understanding where the improvement came from, and where the residual risk now sits. This piece works through what RBI s own publications actually show. Specifically, we draw on RBI s Financial Stability Report (FSR) and its Report on Trend and Progress of Banking in India. We also use RBI s supervisory data releases directly. First, we break the picture down by bank category. Then we connect it to how analysts actually model default risk in practice. What Indian Banking Credit Risk Data Shows About Asset Quality How far asset quality has improved The single most-cited number here is the Gross Non-Performing Asset (GNPA) ratio of Scheduled Commercial Banks (SCBs). RBI s Financial Stability Report was released in June 2026. It put the GNPA ratio of SCBs at 1.8% as of March 2026 a multi-decadal low. RBI s own baseline projection expects only a slight edge-up, to around 1.9% by March 2028. The central bank called this a modest, manageable increase, not a reversal of the underlying trend. That figure looks even more striking against where the system stood less than a decade ago. In 2018, RBI s Financial Stability Report flagged a system-wide GNPA ratio of 11.46%. Banks under Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) RBI s restrictive framework for weak lenders ran even higher. The distance between 11.46% in 2018 and 1.8% in 2026 is the real story here. In fact, it represents one of the fastest deleveraging cycles any major banking system has gone through. And it wasn t accidental. It followed a specific, traceable sequence of interventions. Any credit risk analyst working with this data should be able to name them. Capital buffers moved in the same direction. RBI s June 2026 FSR put the system-wide Capital to Risk-Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) at 17.7%. The Common Equity Tier-1 (CET1) ratio stood at 15.3%. Both are multi-decade highs, per RBI. Similarly, RBI s Report on Trend and Progress of Banking in India 2024-25 shows the same trend over a longer horizon. System CRAR rose from 12.94% in March 2015 to roughly 17.4% by end-March 2025. Profitability tracked the same arc. Scheduled commercial banks aggregate net profit rose too from 2.63 lakh crore in FY2022-23 to 4.01 lakh crore in FY2024-25, per RBI s Trend and Progress data. What stress tests add to the Indian banking credit risk picture RBI s stress testing adds another layer here, separate from the point-in-time ratios above. Under RBI s macro stress test scenarios in the June 2026 FSR, the banking system absorbed hypothetical adverse shocks. Even so, aggregate capital ratios stayed comfortably above regulatory minimums. Compare that to RBI s own 2018 FSR. That report projected a comparable stress scenario could push GNPA at PCA banks as high as 22.3%. It also warned that at least six banks faced a capital shortfall. The gap between those two outcomes, eight years apart, is telling. It may say more about systemic resilience than either year s baseline GNPA ratio alone. None of this means credit risk has disappeared, however. RBI s June 2026 FSR was explicit on this point: new vulnerabilities are building even as legacy NPAs shrink. Specifically, RBI surveyed banks and NBFCs for the report. They flagged rising household debt, rapid growth in gold loans, and AI-enabled cyber threats as their top risks. In other words, the credit risk profile of Indian banking hasn t shrunk so much as shifted. It has moved from the corporate and industrial exposures that dominated the 2PHONE_NUMBER cycle, toward retail and unsecured lending instead. Indian Banking Credit Risk Data by Bank Category and Sector PSBs, private banks, and foreign banks compared Aggregate numbers hide where the improvement actually concentrated, though. RBI supervisory data as of breaks the 2.15% domestic GNPA ratio down by bank category. The Ministry of Finance cited this data in a Parliament reply. Public Sector Banks (PSBs) stood at 2.50%. Private Sector Banks (PVBs) stood at 1.73%. Foreign Banks stood at just 0.80%. Interestingly, the same data shows PSBs improving faster than private or foreign banks since March 2018. In other words, the segment that was historically the weakest link has also recovered the fastest. Even so, it still carries the highest absolute ratio of the three. That PSB recovery shows up in profitability too, per RBI s Trend and Progress report. PSBs aggregate net profit rose from 1.05 lakh crore in FY2022-23 to 1.78 lakh crore in FY2024-25. That s a faster proportional gain than the system as a whole. It s consistent with a segment recovering from a lower base. Where credit concentrates: NBFCs, MSMEs, and smaller lenders Beyond the bank-vs-bank split, this Indian banking credit risk data also shows where credit itself concentrates. NBFC credit is now systemically significant. It reached 14.6% of GDP in FY25, up from 13.5% a year earlier. Industry and retail exposures made up a combined 81.1% share of that NBFC credit as of end-March 2025. Services accounted for the remaining 15.4%. On the bank side, credit to MSMEs grew faster than credit to large enterprises over the same period. Meanwhile, Small Finance Banks (SFBs) posted strong balance-sheet growth. Even so, their asset quality worsened year-on-year, even as their credit-deposit ratio improved to 86.4%. That divergence is telling: large banks and PSBs improving, SFBs under pressure. It s exactly the kind of segment-level signal a system-wide GNPA number alone won t surface. Smaller institutions tell a related story, too. The number of Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) fell by 15 during FY25, to 1,457, as consolidation continued in that segment. Still, UCB credit growth accelerated to 6.7% the fastest pace in six years. Fraud data adds a further wrinkle here. Private sector banks accounted for 59.3% of reported fraud cases by number in FY25. Public sector banks, meanwhile, accounted for 70.7% of the total value involved. Clearly, operational risk and credit risk don t always concentrate in the same segments. How This Credit Risk Data Connects to PD Estimation A GNPA ratio is a lagging, backward-looking measure. It tells you what has already defaulted, not what s likely to default next. That s the gap probability of default (PD) modelling closes. It s also why this Indian banking credit risk data is a genuinely useful input for PD work. It s not just a macro backdrop to quote in an introduction. Two things from the data above feed directly into PD modelling in practice. First, the bank-category breakdown (PSB 2.50% vs PVB 1.73% vs Foreign 0.80%) is a natural segmentation variable. Pooling all SCBs into a single PD model would blur real structural differences in underwriting standards and portfolio.
